{"answers":[{"question_id":"Q004_ferritin_like_functional_divergence","answer":"SCOPe interprets these proteins as divergent homologous families sharing an ancestral structural scaffold, despite their different chemistries. In release 2.08, Ferritin (a.25.1.1; SUNID 47241), Ribonucleotide reductase-like (a.25.1.2; 47253), and Manganese catalase (T-catalase) (a.25.1.3; 100951) belong to the Ferritin-like superfamily (a.25.1; 47240), within the Ferritin-like fold (a.25; 47239) and All alpha proteins class (a; 46456).

The shared superfamily expresses inferred common ancestry, stronger than merely sharing a fold. Fold membership describes structural topology and alone need not imply homology; class membership describes broad secondary-structure composition. Separate families represent more closely related groups within that superfamily, but even family membership does not guarantee identical function. The conserved architecture is an alpha-helical bundle, typically with a four-helix core; SCOPe annotates the superfamily as containing a bimetal-ion centre in the bundle.

Their biological roles have diverged: ferritins form iron-storage assemblies, with ferroxidase-active subunits oxidizing iron for mineralization; canonical class I ribonucleotide reductase R2 proteins generate or maintain the radical machinery supporting nucleotide reduction in the partner catalytic subunit; manganese catalases use a binuclear manganese centre to disproportionate hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. The Ribonucleotide reductase-like family also includes desaturases and monooxygenase components, so its name does not assign ribonucleotide-reductase activity to every member.

Consequently, neither iron-storage function, R2 radical chemistry, catalase activity, nor a particular metal identity can safely be transferred across these families from SCOPe membership alone. Shared ancestry can preserve a scaffold while metal ligands, substrate access, redox properties, and oligomeric organization change. A cross-family structure may provide a template for the conserved core, but not automatically for active-site chemistry or assembly. Specific functional assignment requires additional sequence/profile and structural alignment evidence, inspection of catalytic residues and metal coordination, and biochemical evidence for metal dependence, substrate specificity, and activity. These functional distinctions are pretrained biological knowledge; the live SCOPe evidence establishes the classification and its structural annotation.","evidence_used":["Pretrained model knowledge","mcp__scope__search_scop","mcp__scope__get_scop_node","mcp__scope__list_scop_children","/api/v1/releases/current","/api/v1/releases/2.08/search?q=Ferritin&mode=auto&limit=20","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/a.25.1","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/a.25.1/parents","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/a.25.1/children?limit=30","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/47240","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/47240/annotations","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/47253/children?limit=20"]}]}
